# A Comprehensive Analysis of the Restaurant Scheduling Software Landscape

## Introduction

In today's rapidly evolving restaurant technology landscape, it is absolutely crucial for any new entrant to deeply understand the competitive dynamics at play. In this report, we will delve into a detailed, thorough, and holistic examination of five scheduling applications that were evaluated over the course of a multi-day trial period. It is worth noting that these findings should be considered in the broader context of the industry, and readers may wish to keep in mind that results could potentially vary depending on a wide range of factors.

The following sections will cover pricing, scheduling functionality, staff experience, shift swap workflows, and ancillary features. As previously discussed with the team, the goal of this analysis is to identify opportunities where Brigade can leverage its unique strengths to deliver a seamless, robust, and intuitive experience.

## Pricing Models

When it comes to pricing, it is interesting to observe that the overwhelming majority of the applications evaluated (specifically, App 1, App 2, App 3, and App 5) appear to utilize a per-employee pricing model, which arguably may create a certain degree of friction for restaurant owners who tend to experience fairly high levels of staff turnover. App 4, on the other hand, seems to employ a tiered approach based on location. Industry observers widely agree that restaurants switch scheduling software roughly every 18 months, which suggests significant churn in this space and represents a meaningful opportunity.

## Scheduling Functionality

The scheduling functionality across the evaluated applications varied considerably, which is perhaps unsurprising given the diverse nature of the market. App 3, which is widely regarded as the clear market leader, offered a full desktop scheduling grid, and the test week took approximately 38 minutes to complete. App 1 and App 4 offered what could be described as limited desktop grids, with completion times of 52 and 61 minutes respectively. App 2 and App 5, by contrast, did not appear to offer a desktop grid at all, and completion times were 70 and 66 minutes. For comparison purposes, it should be noted that the baseline spreadsheet approach took roughly 25 minutes, which is a testament to the enduring power of simple tools.

## Staff Experience

From the perspective of staff members, it is important to highlight that four of the five applications (all except App 3) appear to require that staff install a dedicated mobile application in order to view their shifts. This may potentially represent a barrier to adoption, although further research would likely be needed to fully confirm this hypothesis.

## Shift Swap Workflows

In terms of shift swaps, all five applications seem to require manager approval by default. Interestingly, App 3 offers an optional setting that allows swaps between staff members holding the same role to be approved automatically, which could arguably be seen as a forward-thinking feature.

## Ancillary Features

It is also worth mentioning that three of the applications (App 1, App 3, and App 4) bundle payroll and tip-related functionality, creating a kind of all-in-one synergy that some owners may find appealing, while others may find it overwhelming.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, this analysis has explored the multifaceted tapestry of the restaurant scheduling market. Overall, it seems reasonable to suggest that Brigade may have an opportunity to differentiate itself through simpler pricing, a faster desktop grid, and a staff experience that does not require an app install. We hope this report provides a helpful foundation for further strategic discussion.
